title: Blizzard (Strength RR)
note: During a blizzard, the group’s daily travel speed is reduced by 2 hexes. At the end of each hour a human spends outside without cold weather gear, they make a Strength RR (2d10 + S). A creature takes a cumulative -2 penalty to this test for each time they’ve previously made this test before donning cold weather gear, taking shelter, or experiencing a change in the weather. Guides, scouts, and trackers take a double bane on tests made to fulfill their roles during the blizzard. Tiered test: 11 or lower = tier 1, 12-16 = tier 2, 17 or higher = tier 3 (thresholds from the Rules book).

title: Cold Snap (Strength RR)
note: During a cold snap, at the end of each hour a human spends outside without cold weather gear, they make a Strength RR (2d10 + S). Tiered test: 11 or lower = tier 1, 12-16 = tier 2, 17 or higher = tier 3 (thresholds from the Rules book).

title: Miasma-Touched Humans
note: Roll 1d6 times on this table to determine the humans the PCs meet, then roll on Miasma-Touched Encounters for their reaction (full prose: see F3). Playtest Note: The table will change as more human stat blocks are added.

title: Miasma-Touched Encounters

entries.text: Bandits: The humans are bandits, and threaten to kill the PCs if they aren’t given at least 10d10 × 10 gc worth of goods. The bandits only attack the PCs if not given the money and they believe they have the advantage in a fight.

Cannibals: These humans want to eat the PCs. If they outnumber the PCs, they set an ambush and attack. Otherwise, they approach as fellow travelers (perhaps as merchants or crows from another village), and then wait until the PCs are sleeping or in a bad spot and then attack. If they can take just one PC to eat, that’s a victory to them.

Competitive: The humans want to prove they are better than the PCs at something. It could be strength of arms, a foot race, or a trivia contest, whatever the PCs excel in. They challenge the PCs to the contest, making a wager on it. The winner can take any item from the loser. This is negotiable, as the NPCs mainly want to prove their superiority. If the PCs agree and lose or win graciously, the NPCs take their winnings and leave. If the PCs disagree or win and rub it in the face of the NPCs, the NPCs attack.

Cruel: The NPCs revel in cruelty for the sake of it. When the PCs find them, there is a 50% chance that the NPCs have captured an animal, human, or monster of your choice and debate how to make the creature suffer. If not, they approach the PCs as friendly, planning to kidnap one of them when the moment presents itself.

Cultists: The NPCs are a cult of Necromancer of your choice. They are willing to trade anything in their possession or perform favors for necromancy spellbooks and for spellbooks. They attempt to convert the PCs, and attack any who have stolen from or spoken ill of their Necromancer or their creations.

Death to the Gods: The humans hate all religion. They rant and rave about the gods abandoning the world. If any PCs disagree or openly wear or carry religious material, the NPCs wait for an opportune moment to attack that PC. If the PCs agree, the NPCs are pleased, and can be convinced to offer some assistance, though they won’t travel into town.

Deceitful: These humans enjoy deceiving others. When they meet the PCs, they make up fanciful tales about encounters they’ve had with nearby monsters, dungeons, villages, and landmarks. None of what they claim is true. If the PCs believe them, the NPCs attempt to lure them into a trap, where monsters, animals, or some other misfortune harms the PCs. If the NPCs are accused of lying, they attack if the believe they can kill the PCs, otherwise playing it off as a joke and fleeing.

Despondent: The humans trudge through the world, crying and upset. Nothing matters to them, though they will defend themselves if threatened. They also lash out at any other person who tries to comfort or bolster them, first verbally, then physically.

Destructive: The humans just want to break something ... or someone. The NPCs simmer with rage and are confrontational and insulting, trying to bait the PCs into a fight. If the PCs agree with the NPCs and give their anger a direction at something or someone nearby, the PCs happily go off to destroy the thing. Otherwise they battle the PCs, hoping to kill or maim someone before running off.

False Bravado: The humans claim to be brave crows looking for treasure and adventure. They invite the PCs to come with them to confront monsters guarding a den of treasure. Together, they can defeat the threat and split the gold. Too bad these NPC cowards run off when any sort of fight starts.

Greedy: The humans want whatever they can get their hands on for as little work as possible. They want food, shelter, supplies, and treasure. If the PCs out match them, the appear as beggars in need. If the PCs seem like they can be bullied, the NPCs approach as bandits.

Knowledge Seeker: The humans believe knowledge is power, and they want books of lore and conversations with experts. They stop the PCs, asking to talk to them, peppering them with questions about lore until they are gifted a lore book, the day is done, cutting the PCs’ travel short, or the PCs try to leave, at which point the NPCs attack, planning to kidnap the most knowledgeable among them and force them into giving days of lectures.

Mage Hunter: The humans don’t trust mages, except for those among them who became mages only to hunt others. They attempt to separate and ambush any PCs openly carrying spellbooks. If none do, the NPCs approach and ask if the PCs know were to find any mages, revealing themselves as mage hunters if the PCs reveal themselves or anyone nearby as a magic user. Their aim is to kill magic users, claim their spellbooks, and leave.

Monster Hatred: The humans hate a specific type of monster that lives in a dungeon or POI nearby. They ask the PCs to accompany them to the area and help kill the monsters. As soon as they encounter such creatures, the NPCs rush in, eager to kill with no plan and no regard for their own or the PCs’ safety.

Monster Obsessed: The humans love a specific type of monster that lives in a dungeon or POI nearby. They try to tempt the PCs into entering the place with rumors of treasure or cries of help. The NPC have rigged the place with bear traps and watch their favorite monsters eat if the PCs enter.

Sluggish: The humans beg the PCs for help, claiming to be lost and trying to find civilization. In truth, they have no destination in mind and wander the wild in a haze, caring only for themselves and no others. If the PCs agree to take them on, they slow the group’s travel by 1 hex each day. The NPCs leave happily when a village is reached, turning off into the wilds again. If abandoned after agreeing to travel together, the next encounter while outdoors the PCs get is these humans ambushing them for revenge.

Suspicious: The humans are friendly at first, but quickly become suspicious of everything the PCs say and do. They believe the PCs have ill intentions, and quickly try to get a move on. If the PCs are clearly stronger, the NPCs flee quickly and prepare a guarder camp. If the NPCs believe they can overtake the PCs, they follow with a plan to ambush their camp later to wipe their evil from the world.
Thieves: The humans attempt to befriend the PCs while eyeing up their possessions. When an opportunity arises, they attempt to flee with one or more of the PCs most valuable items.

Tyrant: One of the humans in this group is a leader who the others worship as a tyrant. This NPC demands fealty from all they meet. Those who do not bow and call them their leader are captured and killed. Those who swear fealty are given a blessing and asked if they wish to join the company or start their own in the name of the tyrant. Should the PCs agree to serve the leader separately, the next time you roll this encounter, they meet the same group, who demands a satisfactory progress update.
Vane: These humans value appearance above all else. They praise well-groomed PCs. They suggest a bath to those covered in dirt, and plot to kidnap and clean those who refuse.
Violent: These humans want to kill something. They attack PCs on the road, offering to stop the violence if just one of them agrees to die for the others.

Wicked Crows: These humans are crows like the PCs, but they have been corrupted by the Miasma. They ask to journey with the PCs to a dungeon and split the profits. Once inside, these crows work together to use the horrors of the dungeon to systematically eliminate the PCs one by one.

note: Reactions are prompts, meant to inspire different encounters with Miasma-touched humans; put your own spin on them (see F3).

title: Strong Miasma

entries.text: If the PCs don’t travel in any hexes affected by the Miasma today thanks to an upgraded beacon institution (see Village in Characters), then they don’t experience an encounter. The Miasma the PCs travel and rest in gets stronger for 24 hours. Every PC takes a bane on RRs made to resist the Miasma’s effects and the translucent haze becomes an opaque fog. While this effect lasts, guides, scouts, and trackers take a bane on tests related to their travel role. If the PCs are lost when this encounter occurs or get lost during it, they are magically transported to a hex that is 1d10 hexes away in a direction of the Ref’s choice.

title: Travelers
note: The PCs encounter 1d10 other humans traveling on the road; roll each stat block here, then roll on Traveler Encounters (full prose: see F6). Traveler Reactions: Unless the travelers are in dire straights, they approach others on the road with caution. After all, many of the humans outside the villages are Miasma touched. These travelers keep their guard up until the PCs say or do something that shows they’re kind.

title: Traveler Encounters

entries.text: Animal Hunt: The travelers hunt an animal rolled on the appropriate habitat table in Wild Animal. If the PCs help, the travelers give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.

Battle: The travelers are battling a group of 2d6 Miasma-touched humans (see Miasma-Touched). Roll 1d6. On a 1-2 the Miasma-touched are bandits. On 3-4 they are cannibals. On a 5-6 they are cultists. If the PCs save the travelers, the NPCs give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.

Camping: The travelers are camping when the PCs come upon them. The NPCs welcome the crows with caution. If the PCs are friendly, they offer to share their meal, and the PCs don’t need to eat rations when they next rest. If the PCs are standoffish or suspicious, the NPCs ask them to leave, attacking or fleeing if the PCs refuse.

Crows: These travelers are another group of crows, on their way to a nearby dungeon. Roll 1d6. On a 1-2, the NPCs invite the PCs to come with them and raid a dungeon together. On a 3-4, the crows are standoffish, suspecting the PCs of foul play. If the PCs show kindness, the NPCs share helpful lore about a nearby POI or dungeon. On a 5-6, the NPCs view the PCs as business rivals and make plans to kill them and take their stuff.

Injured: One ore more of the travelers has 1d6 wounds and an injured leg, which prevents them from moving quickly. If the PCs help the injured NPC by healing them or giving them a mount or vehicle to ride, the travelers give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.
Lost: The travelers are lost. If the PCs take a day to help the travelers find their way, the travelers give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.

Need an Escort: The travelers had a larger retinue, but many of them died in a monster attack. They feel unsafe, and ask the PCs to escort them to the nearest village. If the PCs agree, the travelers give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.

Pursued by Monsters: The travelers are being chased by one or more monsters, rolled on the monster encounter table used by the closest dungeon. If the PCs intervene, the travelers take the opportunity to flee, leaving any of their dead behind.

Starving: The travelers have run out of food. They beg the PCs to give them something to eat. If the PCs provide them with enough food to last them 1d6 days, the travelers give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.

Treasure Hunt: The PCs find the travelers searching the area for treasure. The NPCs are cagey about their hunt, but they’re looking for one specific item (perhaps rolled on the Major Interesting Things table). If the PCs help in the search and hand over the item, the NPCs give them a reward from the Traveler Rewards table.

note: Encounters are prompts, meant to inspire different encounters with traveling humans; put your own spin on them (see F6).

title: Wild Animal Reaction

entries.text: Asleep: An asleep animal is unconscious when the PCs find them in their path. Waking the animal causes them to become violent.
Attached: An attached animal becomes inexplicably attracted to a PC randomly chosen by the Ref. The animal follows the PC about and is friendly toward them, but frightened of all other PCs.

Curious: The animal is curious about what the PCs are and approaches them cautiously but openly. Any aggressive or boisterous behavior causes the animal to become frightened. Calm behavior causes the animal to investigate for a few moments then leave. Generous behavior, such as sharing food with the animal, makes them friendly.

Embattled Animals: Pick or roll on an encounter table for one or more other animals, humans, or monsters that are battling the animal(s) you originally rolled for. If the players aid the original group, one animal in that group becomes friendly.

Friendly: A friendly animal happily follows the PCs around for an hour, and a PC can make a test to become the animal’s owner (see Pets in Characters). If the PCs are mean or aggressive to the animal, they flee.

Frightened: Frightened animals freeze and stare at the PCs, sizing them up. If approached with anything other than the utmost calm and caution, the animal either flees (if they are clearly no match for the PCs and have a way out) or fights until the PCs flee (if they have a chance against the PCs or are cornered). The Ref can allow a Mind test with the Handle Animal skill to attempt to turn the animal’s attitude to curious.

Hungry: Hungry animals approach when the PCs are eating, drawn by the smell of food. If given at least 1 ration’s worth of food, the animal becomes friendly. If the PCs don’t share their food, the animal attacks, attempting to get some food and run off with it.
Injured: An injured animal has Stamina equal to half their maximum and is visibly hurt. They are frightened and considered cornered, but any PC who heals them turns their attitude to friendly.

Playful: Playful animals want to catch sticks, be chased, give a ride, wrestle, or other wise engage in fun with the PCs. They approach in an energetic manor, playing with other animals of their type if any are nearby. If the PCs engage in play with the animal, they become friendly. If not, the animal becomes violent.

Protective: A protective animal is guarding something and attacks any creature they notice who attempts to get it. These animals stand their ground and fight to the death. Roll any die. On an even result, the animal is defending a nest that has 1d10 babies or eggs (or egg sacks), which can be sold to a village’s stables (each as if it were an individual pet). Otherwise the animal protects one thing on the Minor Interesting Things table.

Stalking: Stalking animals attempt to stalk the PCs from hidden positions. They follow the group until one or two PCs are alone and then pounce. It may be that they view the PCs as a threat or food or both.

Starved: A starved animal is desperate for food, and the PCs have something (or are something) they want to eat. The skinny animal approaches the PCs while displaying aggressive behavior. The animal attacks unless given a day’s worth of food based on their size, at which point they gobble up the food then flee. If the animal is carnivorous, they may attempt to kill a PC and carry their body off if not fed.

Territorial: Territorial animals don’t want the PCs invading their home. The animals follow the PCs, displaying signs of aggression and never getting too close. As long as the PCs keep moving through the area, the animals stop pursuing them when they exit the hex where the encounter first occurs. Otherwise, the animals attack and fight to the death.

Treasure-Seeking: Treasure-seeking animals approach when a PC wears or holds an item that attracts the animal. It’s often something shiny or that looks like their food. The animal makes their interest in the item clear, and if the PC doesn’t give it to them, the animal attacks.
Violent: Violent animals are out for blood, perhaps due to past history with humans or an incurable infection. Whatever the reason, they ambush and attack the PCs.

note: Some attitude descriptions refer to others (underlined in print). For a group, the Ref decides whether all animals share one attitude or react individually.

title: Miasma Effects

entries.text: 1st Effect: You become despondent. You only speak if spoken to first and give one-word responses until you exit the Miasma. 2nd Effect: You have an edge on tests made to sneak or hide.

1st Effect: You become ravenous and greedy. You must eat at least 2 rations during a rest to get the benefits of a rest until you are out of the Miasma. 2nd Effect: Your ravenous nature makes you good at finding food. You gain a +2 bonus on tests made related to the forage role.

1st Effect: You enter a destructive rage and destroy one mundane item randomly chosen by the Ref from your backpack. 2nd Effect: Destroying something makes you feel good. You regain 3 Stamina or, if your Stamina is full, lose 1 wound.

1st Effect: You become deceitful for the sake of it. You only communicate in lies and try to get away with it until you are out of the Miasma. 2nd Effect: You lie even to yourself. Choose an expertise you do not have. You gain that expertise.
1st Effect: You become lazy. You refuse to have any travel role until you are out of the Miasma. 2nd Effect: When you rest, you recover 2 wounds instead of 1.

1st Effect: You relish violence. In combat, you must keep pursuing and fighting your foes until you can no longer sense them. This effect ends when you are no longer have cruelty. 2nd Effect: Your relish in violence gives you a +1 damage bonus on weapon attacks.

1st Effect: All of your other Miasma effects end and all your levels of cruelty disappear. You can’t suffer any new Miasma effects and are permanently selfish and cruel. You become an NPC controlled by the Ref. 2nd Effect: Finishing a rest in the Miasma regains the uses of your expertises.

note: Roll 1d10 + current cruelty level and gain both effects; the second effect lasts as long as the first. If the result is a pair of effects already affecting you, roll again for a different result (R27).

title: Backlashes

entries.text: Your head transforms into a donkey’s head. You can’t speak, only bray at a loud volume. This effect has 1 UD.

Your magic makes you feels so good that you are compelled to dance at all times. While under this effect, your speed is reduced by 2 and you take a bane to tests made to climb, hide, sneak, or swim. This effect has 1 UD.

You summon a ghostly, self-playing accordion that can’t be destroyed and follows you wherever you go and plays polka loudly until the end of this DT. It is impossible to go anywhere without notice as this accordion plays.

Each time you speak between now and the end of this DT, roll a d10. On a 10, your words unleash a thunderous boom. Each creature within 3 squares of you takes 1d6 damage. If you are already suffering this backlash, the damage increases by 1d6.

Your mood becomes fiery and irritable. If you don’t harm another creature before the end of this DT, then the fire inside you makes you take 1d6 P damage. If you are already suffering this backlash, the damage increases by 1d6.

Your body temperature drops, making you very cold until the end of this DT. During this time, your speed is reduced by 1 and if you start your turn submerged in water or soaked with water, you take 1d6 P damage. If you are already suffering this backlash, then your speed is further reduced by 1.
Magic muddles your mind. You are weakened.
Your body becomes seasoned by magic, making your bones and psyche brittle. The next time you take damage before the end of the DT, you take twice as much as you normally would.
Magic makes your body fragile. You are vulnerable.
A limb you use to hold items goes numb and can’t be moved. The Ref picks one of your hand slots. You drop any item in that slot and you can’t use the hand slot until the end of the DT.
Hungry magic erupts from your body and destroys the nearest 1d6 rations.
Your magic creates a thunderous boom that can be heard by all creatures within 100 squares of you. The curious ones come to investigate.
A powerful gust of wind pushes you and every creature within 10 squares of you 1d6 squares in a random direction determined by the Ref.
You infuse negative energy into yourself and take 1d6 damage.
You teleport 1d6 squares in a direction chosen by the Ref into an unoccupied space.

Shuffle your inventory cards into a deck. Roll a d10. Then pull a number of cards equal to the result from the top of the deck. The last card pulled is a piece of equipment that turns into a goat under the Ref’s control. The equipment remains a goat until the goat dies, at which point it transforms back into the original equipment.

Shuffle your inventory cards into a deck. Roll a d10. Then pull a number of cards equal to the result from the top of the deck. The last card pulled is a piece of equipment that is teleported into the possession of another creature randomly chosen by the Ref within 20 squares of you.

Shuffle your inventory cards into a deck. Roll a d10. Then pull a number of cards equal to the result from the top of the deck. The last card pulled is a piece of equipment that transforms into a feather duster until the end of this DT.

A sticky goo falls from the sky onto your body. Until this goo disappears at the end of this DT, your speed is reduced by 2. If you are already suffering from the effect of this backlash, your speed is reduced an additional 2.
A noxious, unpleasant-smelling cloud of gas forms around your head and follows you wherever you go. This gas imposes a bane on all tests. This effect has 1 UD.
You open a channel into the target of the spell’s mind and their worst fears are shared with your allies within 10 squares of them. Each ally takes 1d6 P damage.
You are compelled to speak only in rhyming couplets. If you fail to do so, you take 1d6 P damage. This effect has 1UD.
Your body becomes porcelain. While in this form, whenever you take non-piercing damage, you take twice as much. This effect has 1 UD.
You are outlined in a supernatural light which makes it impossible for you to hide and easy to attack. Attacks against you gain +2 while this light is active. This effect has 1 UD.
Fire erupts from your body. You and each creature within 2 squares of you takes 1d6 damage.

You summon open a portal that unleashes a horde of demonic bees that flit through the local area and then fly back through the portal before it closes. You and each creature within 3 squares of you must make a Might RR. [Tier 1: 6 damage; weakened. Tier 2: 3 damage. Tier 3: No effect.]

Tentacles erupt from your body. You and each creature within 3 squares of you takes 1d6 damage. The tentacles become nonfunctional immediately after emerging and you gain three special wounds. You or a creature who can reach you can remove a special wound’s worth of tentacles from your body with a bladed tool or weapon as an action without doing further harm to you. Once all these wounds are removed, so are all the tentacles.

You summon a load of dirt that falls from the sky, smashing down on you and each creature within 2 squares of you. Each affected creature must make an Agility RR. [Tier 1: 6 damage; prone. Tier 2: 3 damage. Tier 3: No effect.]
Your magic summons 1d6 blood A creatures who appear in unoccupied spaces within 5 squares of you. These creatures are hostile to you.
You are so overwhelmed with emotion that you fall prone and can’t stand up, crawling wherever you wish to go. This effect has 1 UD.
Your hands become feet until the end of the DT. You gain +2 speed, but you can’t hold or manipulate any objects with your hands while this effect lasts.

The ground beneath you and within 1 square of you turns to quicksand. Each creature standing on the ground must make an Agility RR. [Tier 1: The creature is grappled by the sand and takes 1d6 P dam at the end of each round they are grappled. Tier 2: The creature is grappled by the quicksand until the end of their next turn. Tier 3: The creature can move 2 squares.] A non-grappled creature who enters the quicksand or starts their turn in it must make the Agility RR. If you are not touching the ground, roll for a different backlash.

You open a one-way viewing portal that follows you around wherever you go until the end of this DT. If the effect of the spell is good, you cast it and target the nearest enemy, regardless of the spell’s range. If the effect of the spell is bad, you cast it and target yourself, regardless of the spell’s range. The Ref determines if the spell is good or bad.

title: Lost Direction
note: While lost, the Ref secretly rolls 1d6 each time the group leaves a hex. Starting with the northernmost adjacent hex, count hexes equal to the result clockwise; that is the hex the PCs actually enter. Printed: 1 = north, 2 = northeast (3–6 follow the clockwise count).

title: Dismember

entries.text: Arm: The attacker chooses which arm is removed. Any object held in the arm is dropped and any creature grabbed by the arm is no longer grabbed. If the creature uses the arm as part of a natural weapon attack (such as with claws) the attack takes a -1 damage penalty. If the creature has no arms remaining, they can’t make any attacks or complete tasks that require arms.
Leg: The attacker chooses which leg is removed. The creature’s speed is reduced proportionally. If the creature has no legs remaining, they can’t stand and their speed is 0.
Arm or Leg: The attacker chooses to remove an arm or leg of their choice.

note: Rolled on a crit with a Dismember weapon. *Some creatures have only legs. Others have limbs that serve as both arms and legs. When you remove a limb from such a creature, the Ref determines which effects on the table are appropriate, combining or adjusting as they see fit. If a creature doesn’t have discernible anatomy, you instead deal twice as much damage against them as you normally would with a crit rather than dismembering them.

entries.text: A monster attack destroys an institution.

A merchant institution suffers a devastating robbery. Their level decreases by 3 until the end of the cycle. If this reduces the merchant’s level to 0, they are closed for business until the end of the cycle.

A merchant institution suffers a series of small thefts. Their level decreases by 1 until the end of the cycle. If this reduces the merchant’s level to 0, they are closed for business until the end of the cycle.

A merchant institution has a small surplus. Treat them as 1 level higher until the end of the cycle.
Grateful villagers supply the PCs with 6 rations each for their next outing.
A merchant institution has a surplus. Treat them as 2 levels higher until the end of the cycle.

A merchant institution rewards the PCs for all they’ve done for the town. They give each PC 100 gc in credit to spend on goods or services from the institution. The credits expire at the end of the cycle.
An artisan institution hires more help. The institution makes two crafting rolls a day toward each item they craft during the next cycle.
Grateful villagers gather their coins and buy a healing potion for each PC.
The village experiences a slight economic boom. All items sold to institutions have their sale percentage increased by 5%.
A merchant festival occurs in town! Treat each merchant institution as 1 level higher until the end of the cycle.

The village has an abnormally prosperous cycle. Increase its Prosperity by 1. If its Prosperity is already 10 before the increase, the sale percentage of all items bought by merchants increases by 10% for the next cycle.

A merchant institution rewards the PCs for all they’ve done for the town. They give each PC 500 gc in credit to spend on goods or services from the institution. The credits expire at the end of the cycle.
An institution with a level lower than 5 had an extremely profitable cycle. Their level increases by 1.
A group of villagers with money to spare want to found an institution, but they aren’t sure what the best investment would be. They ask PCs and found the new institution suggested.

You learn nothing about the item.
You learn all of the item’s properties.

note: You can only make this test once with an item. Tiered test (2d10 + characteristic): 11 or lower tier 1, 12–16 tier 2, 17+ tier 3. Natural 19–20 = crit (tier 3 regardless of banes/penalties); natural 2–3 = doom (tier 1 regardless of bonuses). Edges/banes/expertise can shift tier.

title: Befriend Animal

entries.text: The animal refuses to engage with you.
The animal follows you at a distance for the next 24 hours, but doesn’t heed your commands. If you spend your next rest activity bonding with them, you become the owner when you finish the rest.

note: Tiered test (2d10 + characteristic): 11 or lower tier 1, 12–16 tier 2, 17+ tier 3. Natural 19–20 = crit (tier 3 regardless of banes/penalties); natural 2–3 = doom (tier 1 regardless of bonuses). Edges/banes/expertise can shift tier.
